141.title: Holi (colors; Prahlada and the fire)
141.hook: the night before the colors: a boy who wouldn't stop saying the name, and the fire that couldn't burn him
141.howItsDone: On the full-moon night before Holi, many Hindu communities light a bonfire for Holika Dahan, retelling the story of Prahlada, walking around the fire, offering grain and coconut, and roasting new wheat or barley; the colors are played the next morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diwali ended: Lakshmi at the open door, a mountain lifted, a sister's blessing. Your line was a mountain held like an umbrella.

The famous photos of Holi show people drenched in pink and green and yellow powder, laughing in the street. But that's the morning. The night before, in towns and villages and temple courtyards, people gather around a great pile of wood and dried branches, sometimes with a figure set on top. At the right moment, it's lit, and the flames go up into the full-moon sky. People walk around it, throw in grain and coconuts, and hold up stalks of fresh wheat to roast. And somebody's grandmother tells the story, again, about a little boy who sat in a fire and walked out.
screen: `BEFORE THE COLORS, A BONFIRE.` → `THE FULL MOON, THE FLAMES.` → `A BOY WHO WALKED OUT OF THE FIRE.`

segments.voice: It starts with a demon king, Hiranyakashipu. After years of fierce austerity, he wins an extraordinary protection: he can't be killed by man or beast, by day or by night, indoors or outdoors, on the ground or in the air, by any weapon. Believing himself unkillable, he orders everyone to worship him. Everyone does, except his own small son, Prahlada, who loves Vishnu and won't stop saying his name. The Bhagavata Purana tells how the father tries everything to break him, or to be rid of him: poison, trampling elephants, snakes, a fall from a cliff. Each time, the boy is kept safe. Then comes the part told at Holi bonfires. The king's sister, Holika, has her own protection against fire. She takes Prahlada onto her lap and sits in a blazing pyre. And the fire goes the other way. Holika burns. Prahlada walks out untouched, still saying the name. Said plainly: the Bhagavata Purana doesn't tell the Holika episode; it lives in other retellings and in the festival itself. But the heart is the same. Soon after, Vishnu comes as Narasimha, half man, half lion, at twilight, on the threshold, and ends the king's cruelty without breaking a single term of his protection. That's why the bonfire is called Holika Dahan, the burning of Holika. People circle it, the way you learned to walk around what's holy on day one hundred and thirty-four, and toss in grain and green wheat from the new harvest.
screen: `A KING WHO THOUGHT HE COULDN'T DIE.` · `A SON WHO WOULDN'T STOP SAYING THE NAME.` · `HOLIKA BURNS; PRAHLADA WALKS OUT.` · `HOLIKA DAHAN: THE BONFIRE.`

segments.voice: Picture the bonfire in front of you, the heat on your face, the full moon above, and quietly name one thing you'd like to put on it: a grudge you're tired of carrying, a fear, a habit of cruelty, even toward yourself. Picture tossing it in and watching it catch and burn down to ash. If you pray, hold a name you honor the way Prahlada held his; if not, hold one steady breath after another, and stay by the fire.
Holi. The spring festival that begins the night before, with a bonfire for Prahlada, the boy the fire couldn't burn. Today's word.
Your line: still saying the name. Tomorrow, the colors come out. That's day one hundred forty-one.

142.title: Holi (colors; Prahlada and the fire)
142.hook: the morning after the fire: Krishna, Radha, a handful of color, and how to play it well
142.howItsDone: On Holi morning many Hindus greet elders first with a touch of gulal and a bow, then play with colored powder and water with family, friends and neighbors, sharing sweets like gujiya; in Braj the celebrations run for days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the night before Holi: the bonfire, and Prahlada walking out of the flames. Your line was still saying the name.

The fire has burned down to ash. Some people carry a little of it home, still warm, and touch it to their foreheads. The next morning, the street belongs to color. Pink, green, yellow, a purple that won't wash out until Thursday. But why color? Nothing in Prahlada's story is pink. For the colors, people tell a different, smaller story, set in a village by a river, about a boy who was worried about his skin. And that story tells you how to play Holi well.
screen: `THE ASH, CARRIED HOME.` → `WHY COLOR?` → `A SECOND, SMALLER STORY.`

segments.voice: The boy is Krishna, growing up among cowherds in Braj, the country around Mathura and Vrindavan. He's dark; the old poems call his skin the color of a rain cloud. The story people tell is that he goes to his foster mother, Yashoda, upset: why is Radha so fair, and I'm so dark? Yashoda laughs: go and put some color on her face, then. So he does, and Radha and her friends put color right back on him. That's the game. It's a story families and songs tell, not a scene from an old scripture. But in Braj it's everything. The towns tied to Krishna and Radha keep Holi for days. In Barsana, Radha's village in the stories, women playfully chase the men from Krishna's village with long sticks, and the men hide behind shields and laugh. In Vrindavan, some temples throw flower petals instead of powder. How do people play? The color is gulal, a soft powder. The old colors came from flowers, like the orange of the palash tree, soaked overnight; some families have gone back to gentle, natural colors. You start with elders: a pinch of color on their feet or cheeks, and a bow. You say happy Holi before you throw. You don't color someone who's said no, or a stranger who's clearly just trying to get to work. Then there's food: gujiya, little fried pastries full of sweet milk and nuts, and cool thandai to drink. The color is a greeting. Krishna didn't throw it to win. He threw it to close a distance, and he laughed when it came back.

Picture walking up to them on Holi morning; you say happy Holi first, wait for them to smile, then a small pinch of pink on their cheek. Then picture them putting color right back on you, both of you laughing, the same messy color.
Holi. The spring festival: the fire the night before, for Prahlada, and the colors in the morning, for Krishna and Radha.

143.title: Navaratri (nine nights, nine forms; Durga)
143.hook: a small red book read aloud before sunrise for nine mornings: three battles, one Goddess, and nine faces
143.howItsDone: During Navaratri many Hindus read or recite the Devi Mahatmya (the Durga Saptashati) across the nine nights and honor the Goddess in nine forms, the Navadurga, one each night, with fasting and prayers; the tenth day, Vijayadashami or Dussehra, celebrates victory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Holi in the morning: Krishna, Radha, and a pinch of color. Your line was color closes a distance.

Before sunrise, in a small kitchen in Kolkata, a grandmother sits on a low stool with a red cloth-bound book open on her knees. She reads aloud in Sanskrit, fast and steady, the way you read something you've read every autumn of your life. A lamp burns beside her. She'll do this every morning until the ninth. Inside is the story from day eighty-seven: the gods' light in one blazing form, a lion to ride, a buffalo demon who kept changing shape. Today, the book itself, and the nine faces the nights are kept for.
screen: `BEFORE SUNRISE, A RED BOOK.` → `READ ALOUD, NINE MORNINGS.` → `THE BOOK AND THE NINE FACES.`

segments.voice: The book is the Devi Mahatmya, the Glory of the Goddess, a Sanskrit text set inside the Markandeya Purana. Many families read it, or have a priest read it, across the nine nights, sometimes whole, sometimes a part each day. It also goes by Durga Saptashati, the seven hundred, after its traditional count of verses. And it isn't one battle. It's three. In the first, the world is all ocean, Vishnu lies in his cosmic sleep, and two demons, Madhu and Kaitabha, threaten Brahma. Brahma praises the Goddess as that very sleep. She lets go of Vishnu, he wakes, and he fights. The second is the buffalo demon you already know. In the third, two demon brothers, Shumbha and Nishumbha, send army after army, and a dark, fierce form, Kali, springs from the Goddess's own brow to meet them. Sleep, a warrior on a lion, the dark one from her brow: in the text, all of them are her. Many Hindus honor her in nine forms, the Navadurga, one a night. Shailaputri, daughter of the mountain. Brahmacharini, the young woman in hard discipline. Chandraghanta, with a half-moon like a bell on her forehead. Kushmanda. Skandamata, mother of the war god Skanda. Katyayani, the warrior. Kalaratri, the dark night. Mahagauri, shining and calm. Siddhidatri, who gives perfection. Traditions differ on details and order, but the idea holds: the same power shows up differently on different nights. In the book, she promises the gods she'll come again whenever they call on her in trouble. Nine nights of reading is one way of calling.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA, READ ALOUD.` · `NOT ONE BATTLE, THREE.` · `NINE FORMS, ONE EACH NIGHT.` · `SHE PROMISES TO COME WHEN CALLED.` · then, large: `THE SAME POWER, NINE FACES.`

segments.voice: Ask what today needs from you, the way the Goddess shows a different face each night: the daughter of the mountain, steady and rooted; the student, disciplined, one more page; the warrior who says the hard thing; the mother, gentle with someone small; or just the calm one. Let one face come. Then breathe as that face for a while, and notice how it sits in your shoulders.
Navaratri. Nine nights of the Goddess, kept with her book read aloud and a different face honored each night.
Your line: wear it on purpose. Gentle or fierce, every face is hers. That's day one hundred forty-three.

144.title: Navaratri (nine nights, nine forms; Durga)
144.hook: a pot of earth with seeds, circles of dancers, dolls on steps, a goddess carried to the river: one festival, kept four ways
144.howItsDone: Many Hindus open Navaratri by setting up a pot as the Goddess's seat and sowing barley beside it, fast on some or all of the nine days, honor young girls as the Goddess in kanya puja on the eighth or ninth day, and keep the nights with garba in Gujarat, Durga Puja in Bengal and golu dolls in the South, ending on Vijayadashami.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Navaratri's book: three battles, one Goddess, and nine forms, one a night. Your line was wear it on purpose.

It's the first morning of Navaratri in an apartment in Delhi. Before breakfast, someone spreads a layer of soil in a shallow tray and scatters barley over it. In the middle goes a clay pot of water, mango leaves tucked around its neck, a coconut on top. A lamp is lit beside it. Then everyone leaves for work and school. There's nothing to see yet, just a pot and some dirt. But by the ninth day, that tray will be a small field of green.
screen: `FIRST MORNING: SOIL AND SEEDS.` → `A POT, MANGO LEAVES, A COCONUT.` → `BY THE NINTH DAY: GREEN.`

segments.voice: It's called ghatasthapana. Ghata, the pot. Sthapana, setting it up. Many families invite the Goddess to be present in that pot for the nine days, and the barley beside it, jau in Hindi, is watched as it sprouts. Then the fast, and people mean very different things by it. Some eat nothing until evening. Many set grain aside for nine days and cook with what's allowed instead: buckwheat flour, water chestnut flour, potatoes, fruit, milk. Some keep only the first and last days. The point isn't hunger. Every meal for nine days reminds you what time it is. You've met the public shapes before: garba circles around a lamp in Gujarat, Durga welcomed in Bengal's pavilions like a daughter home for a few days, golu dolls on steps in the South. Four ways of keeping the same nights. The custom that surprises people most comes on the eighth or ninth day. Many families invite young girls from the neighborhood into the house. They wash the girls' feet, mark their foreheads, seat them like honored guests and feed them, often puri, chickpeas and a sweet halwa, with a small gift at the end. It's called kanya puja, and the girls are honored as forms of the Goddess herself: yesterday's nine faces, sitting on the floor of an ordinary living room. On the tenth day comes Vijayadashami, the victory. Ravana's effigy burns in the North. Durga goes back to the river in Bengal. And in some homes, the green shoots from the tray are shared out as a blessing. The seed went in on the first morning. On the tenth day, you hand out what grew.
screen: `GHATASTHAPANA: SETTING UP THE POT.` · `A FAST THAT KEEPS TIME.` · `KANYA PUJA: GIRLS AS THE GODDESS.` · `THE TENTH DAY: HAND OUT WHAT GREW.` · then, large: `WELCOMED, HONORED, VICTORIOUS.`

segments.voice: Think of one small thing you'd like to see grow, a habit, a kindness, a steadiness, and press it into a tray of soil in your mind like a seed. Breathe beside it. You don't make a seed sprout by staring at it; you keep the nights, and it does the rest.
Navaratri. Nine nights of the Goddess, kept with a pot and seeds, a fast, girls honored as her forms, and the tenth day's victory.
Your line: name the seed you planted. For days the tray looks like dirt, and then it's green. Day one hundred forty-four, done.

145.title: Janmashtami (midnight; Krishna's birth)
145.hook: a whole house awake at a quarter to twelve, a tiny cradle, and a fast that breaks at midnight
145.tomorrow: Ganesh Chaturthi (the clay idol; the immersion)
145.howItsDone: On Janmashtami many Hindus fast until midnight, sing and retell Krishna's birth in homes and temples, and at midnight bathe an image of baby Krishna in panchamrita, dress him, and rock him in a cradle before breaking the fast; children are often dressed as Krishna, and temples set up jhankis, small scenes of the story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Navaratri as it's kept: a pot, sprouting barley, circles of dancers, dolls on steps. Your line was name the seed you planted.

It's eleven forty-five at night, and nobody in the house is asleep. The kids were supposed to be in bed hours ago; they're wide awake. Grandma hasn't eaten since morning. In the corner is a tiny wooden cradle hung with flowers, and in it a little image of a baby. The temple down the road is packed, and people are singing the same few lines over and over, louder as the minutes pass. Someone is watching the clock. At midnight, the conch shells blow, the bells go wild, and everyone shouts. Nothing happened, and everything did. This is Janmashtami. You heard the night itself on day ninety-two; today, how it's kept.
screen: `ELEVEN FORTY-FIVE. NOBODY'S ASLEEP.` → `A CRADLE WITH FLOWERS.` → `AT MIDNIGHT, THE CONCH.`

segments.voice: The story, from the Bhagavata Purana: Krishna born at midnight in Kamsa's prison, carried across the flooded Yamuna, hidden among cowherds. Janma, birth. Ashtami, the eighth day of the dark half of the month, usually in August or September. The festival turns that story into a night you live through. First, the fast. Many people eat nothing, or only fruit and milk, from morning until midnight. It isn't a punishment. It's waiting, with your body. Second, the night. Temples and homes stay awake, singing bhajans and retelling the story, sometimes acting it out, so by midnight you've walked the whole road from the prison to the river. Third, the moment. At midnight the image of baby Krishna is bathed like a newborn, in milk, yogurt, honey, ghee and sugar mixed together: panchamrita, the five nectars. He's dressed in new clothes and laid in the cradle, and people take turns giving it a push. Then the food, often sweets made with butter, because the baby Krishna of the stories is a famous butter thief. And the fast breaks. All evening, the children have their own part. In many homes and schools, small boys and girls are dressed as Krishna, with a peacock feather in the hair and a little flute, and temples set up jhankis, small scenes of the story, the prison, the river, the cradle, for people to walk past and look at. You can't make midnight come faster. You can only stay awake, and be ready when it does.
screen: `JANMA, BIRTH. ASHTAMI, THE EIGHTH.` · `A FAST: WAITING WITH YOUR BODY.` · `THE BATH, THE CRADLE, THE PUSH.` · `A PEACOCK FEATHER, A LITTLE SCENE.` · then, large: `STAY AWAKE, AND BE READY.`

segments.voice: Picture that tiny cradle hung with flowers, in a room full of people who've waited all day, and give it one small push: breathe out as it swings away, breathe in as it comes back, gently, because there's a newborn in there. If you pray, say Krishna's name once with each swing. If not, just keep the rhythm, and wait with everyone else.
Janmashtami. Krishna's birth, on the eighth day of the dark half of the month, kept with a fast, a vigil, and a cradle rocked at midnight.
Your line: stay awake, and be ready. Midnight comes when it comes. See you tomorrow.

146.title: Ganesh Chaturthi (the clay idol; the immersion)
146.hook: a clay Ganesha carried home under a cloth, drums in the street, and a guest who stays only a while
146.tomorrow: Ganesh Chaturthi (the clay idol; the immersion)
146.howItsDone: On Ganesh Chaturthi many Hindus bring a clay image of Ganesha home or to a neighborhood pavilion, invite his presence with prana pratishtha, and honor him daily with flowers, durva grass, modak and arti for one and a half to ten days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Janmashtami: a fast, a cradle, and midnight. Your line was stay awake, and be ready.

In Maharashtra, in late summer, you'll see a family walking home from the market carrying a Ganesha about the size of a toddler. His face is covered with a cloth. A cousin is banging a drum. The kids are shouting Ganpati Bappa Morya. He's made of clay, still slightly damp. At home, a corner has been cleared, a little platform set up, flowers ready. They'll uncover his face only once he's in his seat. For the next few days he's a guest, fed, sung to, visited. Then they'll carry him back out and give him to the water. Today, the arrival.
screen: `A CLAY GANESHA, FACE COVERED.` → `GANPATI BAPPA MORYA.` → `A GUEST FOR A FEW DAYS.`

segments.voice: Chaturthi means the fourth day, the fourth of the bright half of the month of Bhadrapada, in August or September, the day Ganesha is said to have been born. Why clay? Go back to day twenty-two, the first story of camp two. Parvati makes a son from earth, from the paste of her own bath, and sets him to guard her door. Ganesha begins as something shaped by hand. So once a year, families shape him again, or bring home one that's been shaped. At home the image is set on its seat, and a priest or an elder performs prana pratishtha, inviting life into it. From that moment he's treated as present. He gets fresh flowers, blades of durva grass, which he's said to love, and modak, the sweet dumplings he's always holding. Arti morning and evening. Here's a surprise from history. For a long time this was mostly a festival inside homes. Then in 1893, in Pune, the freedom fighter Bal Gangadhar Tilak helped turn it into a great public festival, with Ganeshas in the street, where whole neighborhoods could gather, under British rule, around a god they shared. Today some public Ganeshas tower over the crowds. And you heard on day ninety-three why many people keep their eyes off the moon tonight. The home Ganesha is a guest, and like any guest, he only stays a while: a day and a half in some homes, longer in others. Tomorrow, the leaving.
screen: `CHATURTHI, THE FOURTH DAY.` · `HE BEGAN AS EARTH SHAPED BY HAND.` · `INVITED IN, AND TREATED AS PRESENT.` · `1893: THE FESTIVAL GOES PUBLIC.` · then, large: `A GUEST, FOR A WHILE.`

Put down a small cloth, set him there, lift the cloth from his face, and offer something first: a flower, a sweet, a few blades of grass. Then stay with him a while, the way you'd sit with a guest who's just arrived and has nowhere to be.

147.title: Ganesh Chaturthi (the clay idol; the immersion)
147.hook: after days as a guest, Ganesha is carried to the water, and the crowd asks him to come back sooner next year
147.howItsDone: At the end of Ganesh Chaturthi, after one and a half to ten days, many Hindus perform a final arti and carry the clay Ganesha in procession to a river, lake or the sea for visarjan, chanting Ganpati Bappa Morya; many now use plain clay or immerse at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ganesh Chaturthi: the clay Ganesha carried home, invited in, and treated as a guest. Your line was a guest in clay.

It's the last day. The Ganesha who's been sitting in the living room, fed and sung to, is lifted off his seat. The family does one last arti. Then out the door, into a street that's become a river of people: drums, dancing, colored powder, Ganesha after Ganesha moving slowly toward the sea. At the shore, people wade in up to their waists and lower him into the water. He slips under. And the whole beach shouts the same thing: Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya. Father Ganesha, come early next year. A lot of people are crying.
screen: `ONE LAST ARTI.` → `A RIVER OF PEOPLE TO THE SEA.` → `COME EARLY NEXT YEAR.`

segments.voice: The immersion is called visarjan, from a Sanskrit root meaning to let go, to release. It happens on different days in different homes: after a day and a half, or three, five, seven, and the biggest crowds on Anant Chaturdashi, ten days after Chaturthi. So why make a god from clay, give him a room, feed him for days, and then drown him? Here's how many Hindus explain it. The clay image was never the whole of Ganesha. He was invited into it, and now he's sent off, back to wherever he's always been. The clay goes back to the water and the earth it came from. What was shaped by hand is unshaped again. Nothing is kept on a shelf for fear of losing it. Welcome something fully, then let it go fully: the goodbye is part of the love. There's an honest problem in the modern festival too. Many big images are made of plaster and painted with chemical colors, and they don't dissolve; they pile up in rivers and the sea. So many families have gone back to plain clay, sometimes immersing their Ganesha in a bucket at home and pouring the water on the garden. The old form turns out to be the kinder one. And look at the week you've walked through: Holi's fire and colors, Navaratri's nine faces and nine nights, Janmashtami's midnight cradle, Ganesha arriving and leaving. Four festivals, each one a way of living a story with your hands.
screen: `VISARJAN: TO LET GO.` · `THE CLAY GOES BACK TO THE WATER.` · `WELCOME FULLY, RELEASE FULLY.` · `THE WEEK: FIRE, NIGHTS, CRADLE, CLAY.` · then, large: `THE GOODBYE IS PART OF THE LOVE.`

segments.voice: Picture yesterday's Ganesha, and set in his lap one thing in your life that's had its season: a plan that's done, a role you've outgrown, a worry you've been hosting. Carry him slowly with the drums to the water's edge, wade in, lower him gently, and let go; watch the water close. If you like, say it with the crowd, silently: come again next year.
